title: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS)
subtitle: Read the CT before the nose: the orbit and skull base are millimetres away

sources.title: European Position Paper on Rhinosinusitis and Nasal Polyps 2020 (EPOS 2020)

sources.org: American Academy of Otolaryngology-Head and Neck Surgery Foundation (AAO-HNSF)
sources.title: Clinical practice guideline (update): adult sinusitis
Orbital compartment syndrome: the ophthalmic surgical emergency (Lima et al.)

indications: Chronic rhinosinusitis, with or without nasal polyps, with persistent symptoms despite appropriate medical therapy, as EPOS 2020 defines it, and with CT evidence of disease.
Recurrent acute rhinosinusitis with CT evidence of an obstructed outflow tract.
Complications of sinusitis: orbital subperiosteal abscess, frontal or ethmoid mucocoele, and some intracranial complications in conjunction with neurosurgery.
Allergic fungal sinusitis, biopsy of a unilateral sinonasal mass, and as the access route for CSF leak repair, orbital decompression and dacryocystorhinostomy.
contraindications: Medical therapy not yet adequately tried for uncomplicated chronic rhinosinusitis.
A unilateral mass that has not been imaged with MRI when tumour or encephalocoele is possible. Biopsy of an encephalocoele causes a CSF leak and meningitis.
Uncorrected coagulopathy or anticoagulation that cannot be paused.
A surgeon without image guidance access for revision surgery with lost landmarks, or frontal and sphenoid disease near the skull base, should consider referral.
preparation: A CT of the paranasal sinuses, reviewed by the operating surgeon systematically before surgery, and displayed in theatre. Image guidance for revision or extensive disease where available.
A short course of oral corticosteroid before surgery for polyps reduces bleeding and improves the field in many units; follow local protocol.
Stop antiplatelets and anticoagulants if safe, per local protocol and after discussion with the prescriber.
Consent must include bleeding, orbital injury and haematoma with risk to vision, CSF leak and meningitis, reduced sense of smell, adhesions, recurrence of polyps, and epiphora.
positioning: Supine with the head of the table raised (reverse Trendelenburg) to reduce venous pressure in the nose.
Head turned slightly towards the surgeon on a head ring, eyes taped but visible within the field, never covered by drapes.
The CT and navigation screen in the surgeon's direct line of sight next to the endoscopy monitor.
equipment: Zero and 30 degree (and 45 or 70 degree for the frontal recess) rigid endoscopes, camera, light source, lens cleaner.
Sinus instruments: sickle knife, backbiters, through-cutting forceps, ball probe, microdebrider, angled suction.
Topical vasoconstrictor on neuropatties, local anaesthetic with adrenaline for infiltration, bipolar suction diathermy.
Image guidance system for revision and extended surgery.
anatomy: The uncinate process covers the maxillary ostium and the ethmoid infundibulum. Removing it is the key to the natural ostium.
The lamina papyracea forms the lateral wall of the ethmoid sinus and is paper thin; behind it is orbital fat and the medial rectus.
The skull base slopes downwards from front to back. The lateral lamella of the cribriform plate is the thinnest part, and its height is graded on CT by the Keros classification.
The anterior ethmoidal artery crosses the skull base near the back of the frontal recess and may hang free in a mesentery. Transection lets it retract into the orbit and bleed there.
The sphenoid lateral wall carries the internal carotid artery and optic nerve, which can be dehiscent. An Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell places the optic nerve within an ethmoid cell.
criticalSafety: Review the CT systematically before surgery: cribriform plate depth, lamina papyracea integrity, Onodi cell, sphenoid wall dehiscence, and the anterior ethmoidal artery. Many surgeons teach this as the CLOSE checklist.

Keep the eyes in the field and check them repeatedly. Proptosis, a tense orbit or a dilating pupil during or after surgery is an orbital haematoma until proven otherwise and is treated by the surgeon at once, including lateral canthotomy and cantholysis.
Operate only where you can see. If the field is lost to bleeding, stop, pack, and let the anaesthetist improve conditions before going on.
structuresAtRisk: Orbit and medial rectus via the lamina papyracea
Skull base and lateral lamella of the cribriform plate
Optic nerve and internal carotid artery in the sphenoid
Nasolacrimal duct, anterior to the maxillary ostium
commonErrors: Making a separate antrostomy that does not include the natural ostium, so mucus recirculates and symptoms persist.
Working too high in the posterior ethmoid where the skull base is lower than expected.
Pulling on mucosa or bone attached to the skull base or lamina rather than cutting it cleanly.
Ignoring a small amount of orbital fat. It is a breach of the lamina, and the microdebrider must not be used there.
complications: Bleeding, usually minor; anterior ethmoidal or sphenopalatine artery bleeding can be major.
Orbital haematoma, which can cause blindness through orbital compartment syndrome. Orbital fat exposure, diplopia from medial rectus injury, and optic nerve injury.
CSF leak from skull base injury, with risk of meningitis, which should be repaired at the time if recognised.
Adhesions, recurrence of disease, hyposmia, epiphora from nasolacrimal duct injury.
postop: Head up. Avoid nose blowing and straining for the period advised by the unit.
Nasal saline irrigation from the early post-operative period, with continued topical steroid for chronic rhinosinusitis as EPOS 2020 supports.
Any patient with eye pain, proptosis, reduced vision or a swollen tense eye after sinus surgery is reviewed immediately by the operating team. See the orbital trauma protocol for canthotomy.
Clear watery rhinorrhoea, especially one-sided and positional, is a CSF leak until beta-2 transferrin or beta-trace protein testing says otherwise.

steps.emphasis: The CT stays on the screen for the whole operation. Run the anatomy checklist aloud before the endoscope goes in.
Throat pack recorded on the board. Agree controlled hypotension and total intravenous anaesthesia if the unit uses them to improve the field.
Head up and eyes visible. A draped eye cannot warn you of an orbital haematoma.
Clear the postnasal space with the endoscope. A clot behind the palate is aspirated at extubation.
Count every neuropatty out of the nose as well as the throat pack.
Recovery staff check the eyes as part of observations and know that a swollen, tense eye is an emergency.

step.fess.decongest.title: Decongest and infiltrate
step.fess.decongest.why: Endoscopic sinus surgery depends on the field. Most complications happen when the surgeon keeps operating in a field that is too bloody to see in.
how: Place neuropatties soaked in topical vasoconstrictor along the middle meatus and nasal floor, counted in.
Infiltrate local anaesthetic with adrenaline into the lateral nasal wall at the axilla of the middle turbinate and the uncinate.
Perform a diagnostic endoscopy of both sides and correlate what you see with the CT before any tissue is removed.
pitfalls: Starting surgery before the vasoconstrictor has had time to work.

step.fess.uncinectomy.title: Uncinectomy and middle meatal antrostomy
step.fess.uncinectomy.why: The operation is functional: it restores drainage through the natural maxillary ostium. An antrostomy that misses the natural ostium creates recirculation and fails.
how: Medialise the middle turbinate gently, without fracturing it at its attachment to the skull base.
Remove the uncinate process with a sickle knife or backbiter, staying parallel to the lamina papyracea.
Find the natural ostium with a 30 degree endoscope and a ball probe, and widen it posteriorly or inferiorly, not anteriorly towards the nasolacrimal duct.
pitfalls: Entering the orbit when the uncinate is incised too far laterally.
Creating a second opening and leaving the natural ostium closed.

step.fess.ethmoidectomy.title: Ethmoidectomy from front to back
step.fess.ethmoidectomy.why: The ethmoid labyrinth sits between the orbit and the brain. Working in a defined sequence, with constant reference to the CT, keeps the dissection between those two walls.
how: Open the ethmoid bulla and remove its walls to the basal lamella of the middle turbinate.
Enter the posterior ethmoid through the basal lamella, inferiorly and medially, never high and lateral.
Identify the skull base posteriorly, where it is most reliably found, then follow it forwards, clearing cells from below.
Use through-cutting instruments to avoid stripping mucosa. Avoid the microdebrider near any breach of the lamina papyracea.
Address the frontal recess and sphenoid only if indicated and if the anatomy on the CT is understood.
structuresAtRisk: Optic nerve in an Onodi cell
pitfalls: Losing orientation and continuing. Stop, re-check the CT and image guidance, and find a known landmark.
Assuming the skull base is at the same height posteriorly as it is anteriorly.

step.fess.orbit-check.title: Check the eyes before ending
step.fess.orbit-check.why: Orbital haematoma from an anterior ethmoidal artery injury or a breach of the lamina can threaten sight within a short time. Detecting it in theatre is the difference between a canthotomy and a blind eye.
how: Inspect and gently palpate both eyes: compare proptosis, tension and lid bruising.
Look for orbital fat in the ethmoid cavity. If present, document it and avoid packing that pushes into the orbit.
If the orbit is tense or the eye is proptosed, act now: release the packs, call for ophthalmology, and perform a lateral canthotomy and cantholysis if the orbit is tense and vision is threatened.
pitfalls: Leaving the eyes taped and draped until recovery.
